The worst ranked system I've ever seen, even worse than Apex Legends. Rank doesn't matter, you can be a rookie/bronze and still get against masters/top250 (6-7 levels above you), even though the rank system doesn't allow you to have a friend in your party with a rank too far from yours. Worse is the server you'll get, if you're in USA you can get in EU servers, if you're in EU you can get in USA servers, so you can enjoy the game with a beautiful 150-200ms, it's just a lottery. With this conclusion we can say that there is no ranked system, you just play randomly with restrictions in your party.

Now, the bugs, sometimes the game just doesn't want you to play, before jumping from helicopter, the game just starting to show you some random pictures with the sound of your team fighting, you're somewhere in another dimension. Sometimes the game goes black at the end of the game when you choose to Quit to get back into the lobby, you have to press Alt-F4 and start the game again. Do you hear footsteps? Okay, now try to figure out where, because directional sound is nowhere to be found. Sometimes if your ping is over 150ms you just teleport through walls or windows without breaking them. Not to mention the visual bugs of the weapons were some weapons have the attachments position misplaced for months.

Now, the net code, this is very interesting. The game system will decide whether your bullets will hit the target or not. I have a video where my ping is 15ms (normal battlefield, not RedSec), the person is in front of me (less than 15m) where I shoot him straight in the chest with the aim down sight, and the system decided that I should hit him after the 10th bullet. I killed him after wasting 23 bullets, the weapon was M433, which should kill him with the first 4 bullets at that distance. This is worse in Redsec, where sometimes I waste 30 bullets and barely take down his armor. It's like the system looks at your stats versus the enemy's stats and, if you're much better than them, decides to give them a "chance" :). [h1]🪖 Battlefield REDSEC — Review[/h1]
[hr][/hr]

[h2]💡 Introduction[/h2]
There is a version of REDSEC that could have been genre-defining. A battle royale 
built on Battlefield's twenty-year mastery of destruction and class-based warfare, 
dropped into a market where Warzone is stale and Apex is running on fumes.

What EA delivered is more complicated: mechanically impressive, creatively derivative, 
and wrapped in a monetisation strategy seemingly designed to antagonise the audience 
it most needed on its side. REDSEC is not the disaster its Steam score implies. 
It is also not the revolution the Battlefield name warranted.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🎮 Core Gameplay[/h2]
You hold a riverside house through two rotations. Two squads close in simultaneously. 
Then a tank shell removes the eastern wall entirely. Cover gone. Three seconds to 
reposition using the rubble that used to be your shelter.

No other battle royale does that. Not one.

The ring is instantly lethal — no Fortnite-style zone strolling, every rotation 
carries real consequence. Vehicles dictate match tempo rather than sitting as 
background props. Gauntlet mode, a mission-based squad elimination format, 
is the most distinctly Battlefield thing here — at its best, it plays like 
a heist that keeps going wrong in spectacular ways.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]💥 Tactical Destruction[/h2]
Every other battle royale treats the environment as a static stage. 
REDSEC treats it as a resource both teams are actively consuming.

Breaching a barricade with an Assault charge instead of hunting for an entrance. 
Demolishing a sniper's rooftop from below. Using collapse rubble as improvised 
mid-firefight cover. These are not tricks — they are core skills the game 
actively rewards. The destruction engine feels like the reason REDSEC was 
built in the first place. It is just a shame the rest of the game does not 
always match that ambition.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]⚙️ Class System[/h2]
Consistently underrated and legitimately deep.

[b]Assault[/b] — the only class that can breach heavy barricades; non-negotiable in endgame
[b]Engineer[/b] — the only class that can hack high-security safes holding red-tier loot
[b]Support[/b] — full-health revives and passive squad regen at max Training Path
[b]Recon[/b] — unmatched intel tools for a mode where the ring kills on contact

The Training Path system evolves each class mid-match through completed objectives. 
A squad that plays the mission structure efficiently arrives at the endgame 
meaningfully stronger. That compounding depth is one of the smartest design 
decisions in the current BR market.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]⚠️ Problems[/h2]
EA's execution has been, at times, extraordinarily self-defeating.

Launch netcode failures and bloom inconsistencies created a first impression that 
new players had every right to penalise. Pop-up battle pass ads on every boot, 
aggressive upselling from the $10 base pass to the $25 BF Pro tier, and cosmetic 
pricing that treats earnable content as premium — none of it is unusual for 
live-service gaming, none of it makes REDSEC easier to recommend.

The worst decision at launch: pushing REDSEC challenges directly into Battlefield 6's 
weekly progression UI, forcing paid players into a free-to-play mode they never 
asked for. That is not cross-promotion. That is coercion.

And the honest creative critique stands: the weapon rarity system echoes Warzone, 
revive mechanics mirror Apex. [i]Why here, over the games that built these systems?[/i] 
Tactical Destruction alone is not a complete answer. Thick skin required — 
and not just for the gunfights.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]🏁 Final Thoughts[/h2]
REDSEC set out to blow up the battle royale genre. The destruction engine is 
revolutionary. The class system outclasses most competitors. Fort Lyndon, 
three seasons in, has grown into a map worth exploring.

But a game built on tearing things apart should have had the courage to apply 
that same principle to the formula it inherited. REDSEC dismantles your cover 
and leaves every genre convention standing untouched.

[b]New to battle royale? Legitimate starting point with real strategic depth — 
and it costs nothing to find out.[/b]
[b]Battlefield veteran? Ignore the challenge notifications, lower expectations, 
and give it three matches. The destruction alone is worth the download.[/b]

Three seasons on, REDSEC is finally becoming the game it should have launched as. 
Whether EA has earned back enough goodwill to fill its servers long enough to 
prove that is the more interesting question.

[hr][/hr]

Battlefield 6 had the potential to be one of the best Battlefield games, but right now it has too many frustrating problems.

First, the UI is terrible. Enemy markers, pings, and loadout information are messy and unclear during fights. Sometimes I can barely understand what is happening on the screen because there is too much visual clutter.

Another huge problem is visibility. Enemies are extremely hard to see, especially during chaotic fights. Many times I die because players blend into the environment too much. A competitive FPS should make enemies clear enough to spot.

Gunplay also feels inconsistent, especially on PC. Aiming does not feel smooth and responsive. Controller players currently have very strong aim assist, which makes close and medium-range fights feel unfair against mouse and keyboard players. I am not asking for aim assist on PC, but the balance between controller and mouse feels off right now.

The Battle Royale mode also has strange design choices. Dropping into areas covered by deadly fire zones feels frustrating and unnecessary. Sometimes you are punished immediately after landing, which removes the fun from the start of the match.

Another unrealistic mechanic is being able to open the parachute multiple times over and over. It feels silly and completely kills immersion.

The sad thing is that underneath all these issues, the game actually has potential. The graphics, scale, and Battlefield atmosphere are great. But bad UI decisions, visibility problems, unfair balancing, and questionable gameplay mechanics make the experience frustrating instead of fun.

I really hope the developers listen to feedback and improve the game because right now I cannot recommend it.

Within REDSEC, I still see kids sliding and hopping thinking the game's movement has momentum-based inertia, bunny-jumping out of corners to take advantage of the games low server-tick rate (I don't think a lot of them understand tick-rates to begin with) and getting wiped out without firing a shot because they're scared to engage other players. Military-simulation-esque gameplay especially -- even in an extremely mild, extremely unserious format like the Battlefield series -- gives them an anxiety-ridden disposition. Thankfully most of the bad, pointless mic talk has exited the player-base since the game's launch, but it was definitely there. 

I've got at least 100+ matches in REDSEC by now and I sometimes wonder if people even appreciate how detailed the Fort Lyndon map is. The Battlefield Studios team really took what made, and makes, PubG so understatedely brilliant in terms of level design and brought that to the Battlefield series. A lot of abandoned buildings have their own 'character'; some of the overpasses, broken buildings and destroyed sidewalks will become your 'favorite spots' when you get into the top 6 squads and have to commit to sweatlord-firefighting in the enclosing ring of fire.

The level design in Warzone, Fortnite and Apex have barely approached the level of detail, natural versimilitude and compositional flow that's been put into REDSEC. The visual aesthetics of those three games are in-line with idle-farming auto-clickers and real-life Casino games. 

That's not an insult. 

I'm merely describing what the modern 'gamer' demographic wants: pretty lights and the ability to lose track of time (nihilism and social dishonesty are available and optional). Combat engagements in REDSEC sometimes reminds me Michael Mann's film Heat; intense silence followed by bursts of excitement. The trailers they made for the main Battlefield game and REDSEC are a little exaggerated, but the chaos you see in them can be pretty accurate with respect to what you'll experience while playing.

The first major problem with REDSEC is actually outside of the game's scope. That is, there's a wider level of general ineptitude in the 'gamer' demographic. 

The culture of the times and especially the current gaming scene isn't able to address this lack of discernment (not 'lack of intelligence') in people who participate in video-games. It's my position that this skill-level problem is a downstream effect from newer players being 'priced out' of learning the fundamentals of FPS gameplay. It's especially glaring in the medium-sized REDSEC player-base where you have a lot of newer players to FPS games matched up with experienced vets. 

Very few newer players to Battlefield understand that they have gadgets which can easily mark enemies with a red dot above their heads. They don't understand that spotting, flanking and 'dropping bullets' into enemies is sometimes key to winning an engagement. There are still players (who clearly have more than 40+ hours with the game, judging by their account level) who don't understand how to revive a teammate or who are afraid to engage other players with their fictional, digital gun. 

I sometimes wonder why people 'cheat' in video-games and it's becoming clear to me that people in the gaming demographic, especially in the 2020s, have dulled minds and a cultural refusal to learn and forgive themselves. I conjecture that they believe the Battle Royale format is 'just what everyone does' when they play FPS video-games.

I think the hate for REDSEC is mostly coming from these dull minds. 

A small group of us playing Battlefield appreciate that portions of the map can get hectic and chaotic. That if you constantly shift between aggressively taking a point and painstakingely clearing a point, you'll have a huge impact on the game flow even if you're inevtiably getting stomped. A larger group, however, just wants to spectate a big battle between other players from 2000 virtual meters away...or maybe laugh at all the explosions and funny virtual men jumping around in small spaces...I really don't know. The encouragement to play Battlefield games for this second group seemed to be purely about the emergent character of the games; and that's perfectly fine. The actual game of Battlefield 6 can have a lot of hilarious ♥♥♥♥ going on if you get a good group of players in a match.

The incentives to perform in a Battle Royale game like REDSEC are different, however. They aren't really about spectating those chaotic moments. You'll be rewarded based on your efficiency at positioning, mostly. There's a higher cost in BR games when you play according to your intuition or your willingness to be creative in approaching an enemy squad. Usually you die pretty quickly and then have a long wait to find another match or respawn. That second, larger group has a natural aversion to playing a BR title so they usually quit the match after they die; they're also usually really bad at the game to begin with. 

Rarely are these players putting down damage on other squads. A lot of times when someone quits a REDSEC match it's while they are dead and their teammates are not. Very few of these bad-behaviour players will even use their mini-map when they're alive. It's only when they're dead and spectating that they clearly throw up the big map, but now they're looking for a redeploy point to spam their ghost-pings on (not glancing for red-spot-dots which mark enemy fire). It's actually kind-of funny how pinging in REDSEC mostly happens when players have died; I almost think Battlefield needs a 'spotting' tutorial at this point. 

Listen, I could go on about how the bad player behaviour and the review reception towards REDSEC are very much correlated, but I'll try to wrap it up...

A lot of people will have no kills and are simply trying to slide-jump-run a 'solo' victory by avoiding every squad they encounter. Then they probably write up a negative review and go back to one of the major live-service gaming platforms for their low skill ceiling, low skill floor dopamine hit. I think this all boils down to how a lot of these players, in-game and in discussions of the game, don't comprehend how the Battlefield series' emergent destruction and objective-focused design fit into and elevate a live-service BR game. 

It's really a reading comprehension problem...except in gaming knowledge or something.

Finally, the evolution of FPS games into the high-tension Battle Royale format is geared towards cash-prize competitive play in tournaments; their design is naturally high stakes. They are not based around sitting down and 'enjoying' a Battle Royale match with friends...as much as marketing teams want to convince you otherwise. Advertising is more effective than people think and a lot of players are deluding themselves when it comes to their happiness and fulfillment when they pick up REDSEC.

You'll see REDSEC with a ton of negative reviews, but only a very small handful of them are deserved. This is a great BR game; that's coming from someone who thinks PubG is the only true BR game (and I don't even like PubG that much).

The fact is a lot of younger players and 'aged-out' players in the gaming demographic just don't have the stored up wisdom to play video-games (or consume the vast majority of entertainment products, for that matter). It's been really hard for DICE / Battlefield Studios / EA to revitalize this series and it's clear to me at this point it's a cultural problem with the community, not necessarily a game development problem. 

It's unfortunate that a lot of these people are alienated from REDSEC's semi-realistic gameplay: there's a great game here if you really dig in. This is probably one of the better live-service FPS games I've played in my lifetime, but despite its focus on emergent combat, realistic movement and bullet physics...it is still a live-service Battle Royale game; if you're not into BR stuff, just stay away.
